extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy, and the philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of what counts as proof/inference and the role and limits of definitions and postulates in demonstrative reasoning; distinguishes apparent from real inference and characterizes induction and ratiocination. Intended as a textbook-level account for learners of formal and philosophical logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are properly of names only
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions state the meaning of words (names) rather than assert facts about things; the only conclusions that can follow from a definition, strictly construed, are propositions about the meaning of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Replacing 'is' with 'means' avoids treating definitions as factual premises. A definition of 'dragon' yields only conclusions about word-meanings, not about real serpents breathing flame. Thus definitions do not, by themselves, serve as premises for demonstrative truths about real objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postulates implied in definitions supply the real premises
rubrics_metrics.description: When a definition appears to function as a premise in demonstration, the actual premise is a tacit postulate implicit in the definition (for example, the postulate that a figure with equal radii can be described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: In Euclidean constructions the ability to 'describe' a circle is not given by the definition but by a postulate that such a figure may be made to exist. Whether these postulates rest on intuition or proof is debatable, but they are the premises on which theorems depend; definitions alone could be dispensed with without affecting demonstrative certainty so long as the postulates remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make tacit existence assumptions explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a reasoning step about Things (not merely ideas or words) is made using a definition, one tacitly assumes the real existence of an object conformable to that definition; this assumption must be recognized as a distinct premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexample: Defining 'dragon' as 'a serpent breathing flame' leads to a valid syllogism whose conclusion would be false if one tacitly assumed dragons exist. To avoid error, either add the premise that such an object really exists or reformulate to speak about meanings or ideas ('means' or 'the idea of').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish reasoning about ideas from reasoning about things
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions that pertain to ideas require only the assumption that such ideas exist in the mind; conclusions about Things require assuming the real existence of corresponding objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show three parallel forms: (a) statements about words/meanings (true when reformulated with 'means'), (b) statements about ideas (true given existence of the idea), and (c) statements about things (require postulate of real existence). Be explicit which level a premise/conclusion addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent inference vs real inference
rubrics_metrics.description: An ostensible inference is not real when the conclusion is merely a restatement or part of what was already asserted in the premise(s); such cases include equipollency/equivalence, universal→particular instantiation, and when the consequent merely connotes what the antecedent connotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'No man is incapable of reason' for 'every man is rational'; 'All A is B' therefore 'Some A is B'; 'Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is a living creature' (predicate already connoted). These cases do not produce genuinely new truths and should not be treated as proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion and its limits (conversion per accidens and contraposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion (turning predicate into subject and vice versa) can sometimes produce a true translated proposition, but often only by weakening universality or changing terms; it is often a reiteration rather than a genuine inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules and examples: Some A is B → Some B is A; No A is B → No B is A; All A is B cannot be converted to All B is A but converts to Some B is A (conversion per accidens). Some A is not B converts only by contraposition into 'something which is not B is A' after rephrasing. Such conversions are useful but do not create new facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for genuine inference
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine inference occurs when the conclusion asserts something truly distinct from, and not already contained in, the premises — i.e., the conclusion goes beyond mere re-assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test to separate real proofs from mere reformulations. Genuine inference is the kind targeted by the science of logic; apparent inferences (equivalences, conversions that only reword) should be filtered out when evaluating reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of reasoning: Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is inferring a proposition more general than the premises; it proceeds from less general propositions (particulars or lower generals) to higher generalities or laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic: the inductive conclusion 'embraces more than is contained in the premises' and thus is a real inference. Induction includes moving from many individual instances to a general law or from several general propositions to a still more general one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of reasoning: Ratiocination (Syllogism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratiocination or syllogistic reasoning infers propositions of equal or lesser generality from given general propositions, often by combining premises to derive a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratiocination is typically reasoning from generals to particulars (or to equally general propositions). Note that nothing new can be derived from a single general proposition alone without combination with others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propositions analyzed by their ultimate content
rubrics_metrics.description: The real subject of every proposition is facts/phenomena of consciousness or hidden causes/powers; what is predicated of them is one of: Existence, Order in Place, Order in Time, Causation, or Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This taxonomy is a theoretical foundation for understanding what propositions assert and for determining which propositions are susceptible to proof (those not amenable to direct consciousness or intuition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good definition: compatible with usage and focused on important attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: When defining a general name, aim to preserve its capacity to denote most important or numerous members of the class and to fix a distinct connotation by specifying common and significant attributes (differentiæ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: prefer differentiæ that lead to the greatest number of interesting propria; definitions should balance continuity with established usage and philosophical clarity. Where spontaneous usage is vague, restrict denotation so the name regains utility for thought and communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language 'grown' by usage requires logical mending
rubrics_metrics.description: Since language develops organically rather than being designed, many general names have vague or overextended denotations; logical inquiry often requires refining or narrowing such names to make them serviceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat existing classifications as valuable empirical material. When a name connotes nothing precise due to successive extensions, the remedy is to confine it to objects possessing some common attributes—effectively 'mending' the language for clearer thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of training in conversion and opposition of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even though many exercises in conversion and opposition are restatements, training in these techniques cultivates the intellectual habit of recognizing the identity of assertions under diverse wordings, an indispensable logical skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical note: manuals for students should cover these topics thoroughly because they develop circumspect interpretation and precision in measuring the extent of assertions; technical distinctions (contradictory, contraries, subalterns, etc.) assist in this cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware idealized postulates versus empirical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulates used in demonstrative sciences may not be exactly true in nature (e.g., a circle with radii exactly equal does not exist), yet as much of the postulate as is needed to support the true part of the conclusion suffices for demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical implication: recognize idealization in premises and ensure that the portion of the postulate employed legitimately supports the corresponding aspects of the conclusion; this resolves apparent paradoxes about certainty resting on imperfect premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry into definition may require empirical and deep analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the proper meaning of many abstract general names is often a deep inquiry into the properties of the things named (usage, whether they form a class, shared attributes), not a mere comparison of authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence of investigation: (1) assess whether usage is consistent enough to permit inquiry; (2) determine whether the objects truly form a class; (3) identify common attributes; (4) if no natural class exists, consider artificial classification to make the name useful. Such inquiries can lead to significant philosophical investigations.
